name: Coffee
summary: How Filipino smallholders raise coffee from a bagged seedling to the first real picking, mostly Robusta in the lowlands and middle hills, Arabica in the cool uplands, and Liberica (barako) and Excelsa in between. It is written for backyard and small farm growers who plant a few hundred trees under coconut, fruit trees or kakawate shade.
season: Trees go into the field as the rains begin, usually June to August in Luzon and the Visayas, on a cloudy day. In parts of Mindanao where rain falls through most of the year, farmers plant whenever the rains are steady. Seeds are sown in the nursery about a year earlier. The main picking months are the cool months, roughly November to March.
material: Most farmers plant bagged seedlings about a year old, with six to eight pairs of leaves, raised from the seeds of ripe red berries picked from their best bearing trees, or bought from a known nursery. The berries are pulped, washed and the beans sown fresh, because old coffee seed loses its life fast. Some buy grafted or rooted Robusta and Arabica for even, early bearing. A month or two before planting, the seedlings are moved into more sun to toughen them.
spacing: Robusta about 2 m x 3 m alone, or 3 m x 3 m when bananas or other crops share the field. Arabica about 2 m x 2 m alone, or 2 m x 3 m with vegetables between the rows. Liberica (barako) and Excelsa, the biggest trees, about 3 m x 4 m alone or 4 m x 4 m with other crops. One seedling a hole.
water: Almost all coffee here is rain fed: planting is timed to the start of the rains so the young trees have months of water to root. Seedlings planted late are hand watered through the first dry months, and mulch keeps the soil damp. Older trees need a dry spell to flower and get no watering.
fertilizer: Compost, chicken manure and rotted coffee pulp are the usual feeds, a few kilos a tree in the planting hole and again each year. Farmers who buy fertilizer use complete fertilizer (14 14 14) at planting, then complete fertilizer or urea (46 0 0) twice a year, early in the rains and near their end, spread in a ring under the edge of the leaves. Many smallholders give little or nothing, and their yields show it.
care: Ring weeding three to four times a year, mulch under the trees, pulling off upright suckers from the trunk, and bending young stems to grow three or so trunks. After each harvest, farmers cut out dead and drooping branches. Old trees of 10 years and more are cut back low, about 30 cm from the ground, and a new sucker is grown into a fresh trunk.
harvest: Berries are ready when they turn fully red, about eight to ten months after flowering. Trees first bear in the third year after planting. They are picked by hand over several rounds, kept off the ground, and sun dried whole on mats or raised trays until hard and rattling, then hulled to green beans and stored dry in clean sacks.

ways.label: Bagged seedlings (punla sa supot)

steps.title: Set up shade a year ahead
steps.how: Where there are no coconut or fruit trees yet, plant kakawate stakes, banana or other shade trees about a year before the coffee. Coffee likes filtered light, not full open sun, especially in hot lowland farms.
steps.tip: Do not plant the shade at the same time as the coffee. It will not be big enough to help.

steps.title: Sow fresh seeds in a seedbed
steps.how: Pick fully red berries from your heaviest bearing trees, remove the pulp, wash the beans and sow them flat side down in a bed of sand or fine loam under shade. Keep the bed moist. Sprouts come up in about six to eight weeks.

parts.title: Pick seed berries from your best trees
parts.how: Choose fully red, sound berries from healthy trees that bear heavily and show no pest or disease. About three quarters of a kilo of seed plants a hectare, so gather about half again as much to cover seed that fails and gaps to refill later.

parts.title: Pulp and soak the beans
parts.how: Squeeze the skins off by hand or pass the berries through a pulper, then leave the beans under clean water for about a day so the slippery coat loosens.

parts.title: Wash and throw out the floaters
parts.how: Rub and wash the beans clean, stir them in fresh water and skim off every bean that floats. Keep only the heavy seed that stays at the bottom.

parts.title: Dry the seed in the shade
parts.how: Spread the washed seed thinly on a raised tray or in a shaded, airy room and let it air dry for about four days, with its parchment skin still on. Never dry seed in hot sun.
parts.tip: Sow it soon after: coffee seed loses its life within a few months of picking.

parts.title: Make a raised seedbed
parts.how: In a shaded spot, raise a bed about 1 m wide and about 15 cm high. Fill the top with loose soil mixed about half and half with river sand, because heavy red soil alone packs too hard for the sprouts.

parts.title: Sow flat side down
parts.how: Water the bed, then draw shallow lines about 1 cm deep and about 10 cm apart across it. Lay the beans flat side down about 2 cm apart along each line and cover them thinly with the same mix.

parts.title: Mulch and keep it damp
parts.how: Cover the bed with rice straw and water it gently so the seed stays damp but never soggy. The first roots push out after about three to four weeks, and the stems lift the seed caps out of the soil some weeks later.
parts.time: about 25 days to the first sprouts

steps.title: Move sprouts into bags
steps.how: When the two round seed leaves open, lift the young plants gently and set each one in a plastic bag of garden soil mixed with compost or rotted manure. Keep the bags under partial shade and water them often.
steps.tip: Throw away seedlings with bent or curled roots. They grow poorly in the field.

parts.title: Mix fresh potting soil
parts.how: Sieve fertile topsoil and mix about five parts of it with one part of dry manure or compost. Use new soil each time, never soil from old bags, which can carry the fungus that makes young seedlings fall over and die.

parts.title: Fill and wet the bags
parts.how: Fill black plastic bags of about 6 by 8 inches that have small holes for drainage. Water them well before moving the seedlings, so the soil settles.

parts.title: Lift them at the butterfly stage
parts.how: Move the seedlings when the two round seed leaves have just opened, or earlier while the stem still stands straight like a matchstick. Lift each one with a stick or trowel so the roots do not tear, and keep only those with a straight taproot and plenty of fine roots.
parts.tip: A root bent like the letter J never straightens, and that tree stays weak in the field.

parts.title: Plant at the same depth
parts.how: On a cool, cloudy day, poke a hole about 5 cm deep in each bag, set the seedling in and lift it a little so the root hangs straight. Firm the soil at the same depth it grew in the bed and water it.

parts.title: Line the bags up under shade
parts.how: Stand the bags in rows inside a bamboo or wooden frame so they do not tip over, under a roof of bamboo slats, branches or shade net that cuts about half the sun. Pull weeds and water to keep the soil damp, never soggy.

parts.title: Give the seedlings room
parts.how: As the plants grow, move the bags apart so the leaves do not crowd each other, or the seedlings grow tall and thin. Take out any bag with a sick or dead plant.

steps.title: Clear, stake and dig the holes
steps.how: Slash the weeds, keep any tree that can give shade or break the wind, and stake a straight line along the edge of the field. Dig holes about 40 to 60 cm wide and deep, fill them back with the topsoil mixed with compost, and leave them to settle until planting.

parts.title: Run a base line
parts.how: Stretch a straight line along one edge of the field and stake every planting spot from it at your spacing, for example 2 by 3 m for Robusta grown alone.

parts.title: Dig the holes
parts.how: Dig each hole about 40 cm wide, long and deep, or up to about 60 cm each way, so the young roots spread easily. Keep the dark topsoil on one side.

parts.title: Fill back with topsoil and compost
parts.how: Mix the topsoil with compost and return it to the hole, so the seedling roots into loose, fed soil.

parts.title: Let the holes settle
parts.how: Leave the filled holes for about two months before planting, so the soil settles and the compost starts to feed the soil.

steps.title: Harden the seedlings
steps.how: One to two months before planting, move the bags into more sunlight and water a little less, so the leaves toughen before they face the field.

parts.title: Open the shade little by little
parts.how: About two months before field planting, start thinning the shade a little at a time, so the seedlings get used to full light over several weeks.

parts.title: Water a little less
parts.how: Give the bags less water than before, enough to keep the plants from wilting, so the leaves and stems toughen.

parts.title: Check that they are ready
parts.how: A seedling is ready for the field when it has six to eight pairs of leaves, which takes about a year from sowing.

steps.title: Plant at the start of the rains
steps.how: Pick a cloudy day once the rains are steady. Water the bag well, cut away the plastic, set the seedling straight up in the hole at the same depth it grew, and firm the soil around it with your feet.
steps.tip: Avoid hot, windy days and the middle of the day.

steps.title: Give the first feed
steps.how: Many farmers mix 2 to 5 kg of compost into each hole, and those who use bought fertilizer add a small handful of complete fertilizer (14 14 14), about 75 g a tree, worked into the soil away from the stem.

steps.title: Mulch around the young tree
steps.how: Spread rice straw, dry grass or coffee pulp about 5 to 8 cm deep in a circle around the seedling, leaving a small gap at the stem. It keeps the soil damp and holds weeds down, which matters most as the rains end.

steps.title: Replace the dead ones
steps.how: Walk the rows a month after planting and fill any gaps with spare seedlings from the nursery while the rains still last.

steps.title: Ring weed under each tree
steps.how: Pull or slash the weeds in a ring under each tree and leave them as mulch. Most farmers do this three to four times a year, more often in the wet season.

steps.title: Pull off upright suckers
steps.how: Rub or cut off the upright shoots that keep coming from the main trunk, so the tree puts its strength into the side branches that will bear.

steps.title: Feed again as the rains end
steps.how: Farmers who fertilize usually feed twice a year, once early in the rains and once near their end, scattering compost, manure or complete fertilizer in a ring under the edge of the leaves and covering it lightly.

steps.title: Bend the stem for more trunks
steps.how: Many Robusta and barako growers bend the first young stem down and tie it to a stake, so three to five new upright shoots come up along it. When they reach about 30 cm, keep the three strongest as main trunks and cut off the old bent stem.
steps.tip: Farmers who keep one trunk instead top it at about 1.6 m in the third year.

steps.title: Clean the lower branches
steps.how: Cut back branches that droop and touch the ground, and remove dead, weak or pest damaged twigs, so light and air reach inside the tree.

steps.title: Watch the flowers and young berries
steps.how: The trees flower after a dry spell and the berries need about eight to ten months to ripen. Look for tiny holes at the tip of green berries, a sign of the berry borer, and pick up fallen berries so the pest has nowhere to breed.

steps.title: Pick only the red berries
steps.how: The first real picking comes in the third year, about 36 months after planting. Go through the trees several times in the season and pick only the fully red berries by hand, leaving the green ones to ripen. Twist each berry off without tearing the stalk so next year's flower buds stay.
steps.tip: Keep picked berries in clean sacks or baskets, off the ground, and process them the same day.

steps.title: Dry and hull the beans
steps.how: Most small farmers sun dry the whole berries on mats, nets or raised trays, turning them often and covering them at night and in rain, until the beans rattle inside the dry skin. Then they are hulled and kept in clean sacks off the floor in a dry room.

parts.title: Sort the berries the same day
parts.how: Pour the picked berries into water and skim off the ones that float, which are light, dry or bored by insects. Pick out green, black and overripe berries by hand.
parts.tip: Never mix fresh berries with yesterday's berries that have started to ferment, or the whole lot spoils.

parts.title: Start drying within 12 hours
parts.how: Spread the berries to dry within about half a day of picking, so they do not sour in the sack.

parts.title: Spread them thin and off the ground
parts.how: Lay the berries on raised bamboo or net trays, or on a clean cement floor, never on bare soil, in a layer no deeper than about an inch. Beans dried on the ground pick up dirt and taste of grass.

parts.title: Rake two or three times a day
parts.how: Stir or rake the berries two or three times a day so they dry evenly, and pile and cover them at night and whenever rain comes.

parts.title: Dry for two to three weeks
parts.how: Sun drying takes about two to three weeks for Robusta and Arabica, and about three weeks for the big Liberica (barako) and Excelsa berries. The moisture should come down to about 12 to 14 percent.

parts.title: Shake to test
parts.how: Shake a handful of berries: when they rattle, the beans are dry. Stop there, because overdried beans turn brittle and break at the huller, and damp ones grow mold in storage.

parts.title: Hull, sort and store
parts.how: Hull the dry berries, then pick out black, broken and moldy beans by hand. Keep the green beans in clean sacks on pallets in a cool, dry room.

parts.title: Or make washed coffee
parts.how: Farmers who sell washed coffee remove the pulp within a day of picking, let the wet beans ferment in a tank of water for about 18 to 24 hours, wash them clean and then dry them the same way.

ways.note: The first real picking comes in the third year after field planting, about 36 months (1,080 days). Arabica on a good site can start a little earlier.

mistakes: Planting in full open sun in hot lowland farms with no shade.
Leaving the plastic bag on, planting too deep, or setting the seedling at an angle.
Never pruning, so the trees grow tall, crowded and hard to pick.
Stripping green, red and dry berries together, which spoils the taste and the price.
Drying berries on bare soil or the roadside where they pick up dirt and mold.
Sowing seed from unknown or weak trees.
better: Plant grafted or clonal seedlings of a good variety from an accredited nursery.
Test the soil and feed by the result, with lime where the soil is very sour.
Keep light shade, prune every year after harvest, and cut back old trees to renew them.
Pick only ripe red berries and dry them on raised beds to sell for a better price.
Scout for the berry borer and other pests, pick up fallen berries, and use integrated pest management.
Match the type to the place: Arabica in the cool uplands, Robusta, Liberica or Excelsa lower down.

watering.traditional: Nearly all coffee here is rain fed: seedlings are watered often in the nursery, planted on a cloudy day once the rains are steady, and after that left to the rain under shade and mulch. Grown trees are not watered at all, because they need the dry months to flower.
watering.method: A watering can with a rose for the seedbed and bags, and a pail into the mulched ring for young trees in the field. Grown trees get rain only. A few farms with a spring or tank run sprinklers to start flowering. Water in the early morning or late afternoon.
watering.rainfed: Plant on a cloudy day once the rains are steady, under shade trees such as kakawate, banana or coconut, and keep 5 to 8 cm of straw, dry grass or coffee pulp around each tree. On slopes, dig short trenches along the contour between the rows to catch the rain. Shade and mulch keep the soil cool and damp enough for coffee to get through the dry months without watering.
watering.dryseason: Young trees in their first dry season: once or twice a week where the soil dries, more on open slopes. Bearing trees: no water until flowering is due, then, where water is at hand, one heavy soaking to bring on the bloom and a few more for about three weeks after. Water a young tree when its leaves droop at midday and are still limp in the evening.
watering.wet: Coffee does not stand waterlogged soil: plant with the collar a little above the ground and drain flat, wet spots. Rain in the middle of the dry spell brings early, scattered flowering and an uneven harvest. Wet, crowded, heavily shaded trees get more leaf rust, so prune after harvest to let air through.

schedule.often: Every day or every other day in dry weather
schedule.amount: A light sprinkle from a rose can, enough to keep the sand damp all the way down
schedule.why: Fresh coffee seed takes six to eight weeks to sprout and dies if the bed dries.

schedule.often: Every day in dry weather, every 2 to 3 days in cloudy weeks
schedule.amount: Enough to wet each bag right through
schedule.why: Bagged roots cannot reach any water outside the bag.

schedule.often: A little less often, every 2 to 3 days, as the bags move into the light
schedule.amount: Enough to keep the bags from wilting. Soak them well the day before planting
schedule.why: Tougher leaves stand the field better.

schedule.stage: Planting to the end of the rains
schedule.often: Rain is usually enough. Water only in a dry week
schedule.amount: One good soak of the mulched ring around the tree
schedule.why: Planting with the rains gives the roots months of water to spread.

schedule.often: Once or twice a week for trees planted late or on dry, open slopes
schedule.amount: Enough to soak the mulched ring a hand deep
schedule.why: Young trees are lost in their first dry months more than at any other time.

schedule.often: Left to the rain. Water only young trees that wilt in a long dry spell
schedule.amount: A soak of the ring under the leaves
schedule.why: The roots are deep enough by now to ride out a normal dry season.

schedule.stage: Bearing trees: dry spell before flowering (each year)
schedule.why: The flower buds need some weeks of dry weather to be ready to open.

schedule.often: Where water is at hand and the rain comes late, one heavy watering or sprinkler run breaks the dry spell. The trees bloom about 7 to 12 days later
schedule.amount: A soaking like a good heavy shower over all the ground under the trees
schedule.why: A dry spell broken by rain or water makes the whole farm flower together.

schedule.often: Keep the soil moist for about three weeks after blooming, watering about once a week if no rain falls
schedule.amount: The same soaking under the trees
schedule.why: Without a follow up shower, many young berries drop.

schedule.often: Rain usually covers it. Water only in a long dry spell
schedule.amount: A soak of the mulched ring under the leaves
schedule.why: Thirst while the berries fill gives black, shrunken beans.

critical: The seedbed and the bags in the nursery, which must never dry out.
The first dry season after planting, when young trees die without mulch or water.
The three weeks right after flowering, when a dry spell drops the young berries.
Berry filling, since lack of water then gives black, shrunken beans.

signs.dry: Leaves droop and curl at midday and stay limp in the evening, older leaves yellow and fall, few flowers open, young berries drop, and at harvest the beans come out black and shrunken.
signs.wet: Yellow leaves, rotting roots and branches dying back on waterlogged ground, and flowering in small scattered rounds after off season rains.

better: Where a spring or tank is near, one heavy sprinkler run at the end of the dry spell and a follow up about three weeks later give one even flowering and a bigger, easier harvest.
Keep the shade trees and the thick mulch. They hold more water in the soil than any watering a small farm can manage.
